NEW YORK CITY COUNCIL STATED MEETING 73 lives of countless New Yorkers. It addresses an issue that too often goes unnoticed until it's too late— concussions, traumatic brain injuries, and the longterm risks associated with repeated head impacts, including CTE. Most people think of CTE as something that only affects professional athletes, but the truth is, it affects young athletes, recreational players, and many of our own city employees working in physically demanding or high-risk jobs. And tragically, here in New York City, we were reminded of the stakes in July when the Midtown shooting involved an individual who believed untreated head trauma had caused his mental decline. Nothing excuses violence, but it really showed how critical it is to take this issue seriously. What we lack right now is awareness. In fact, in the Netflix documentary about Vince McMahon, I was very surprised to see how many professional athletes questioned whether CTE is even real. If that's where the understanding is, we have a lot of work to do. So this bill focuses on exactly that. It creates a citywide public education campaign so families, coaches, and workers know the signs of concussions and where to get help. It makes

And it requires A recurring report so we can understand the trends and shape smarter policy moving forward. It doesn't ban sports, and it doesn't interfere with privacy; it simply gives people the information they need to protect themselves and the people they care about. So I'm proud to introduce this legislation. I think it complements some legislation the Council's already passed. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you so much. Today, I'm excited to introduce Bill Number 1495. It's the Doula Bill of Rights. This legislation is the next step in our large effort to strengthen birth justice in New York City. Earlier this session, we passed the citywide Doula Program to codify and expand access to doula support across our communities. And now we're making sure the people who

NEW YORK CITY COUNCIL STATED MEETING 75 provide that care, that service, that they are respected, they are recognized in these places—they go to work, they are protected, and that they are listened to. The bill reflects years of conversations I've had with doulas, midwives, birth workers, and new parents. Again and again, they told us that the system can feel opaque, inconsistent, and at times, downright hostile to the very people supporting families through one of the most vulnerable moments of their lives. The Doula Bill of Rights aims to bring clarity, accountability, and dignity into that space. Under this legislation, the Commissioner of Health and Mental Hygiene will be required to develop and publish a clear, accessible list of rights for doulas working in hospitals. These rights will help ensure that doulas can do their job safely, collaboratively, and without unnecessary barriers, and that birthing people know exactly what they're entitled to expect. The bill also creates a formal feedback channel, a submission form for doulas to share concerns, experiences, and recommendations directly with the City.
